# The host language

The 1446 book had no host language to explain: its letters were the whole
system. gog's letters live inside four programming languages, and this
part is what that costs.

Everything so far has been the grammar, and the grammar is the same
wherever you write it. One engine reads one specification, so the same
sentence draws the same plot in every language.

This part is what is left over. Some things belong to the language you
type in rather than to the grammar, and they cannot be stated once for
everybody. A table has to reach `data()`. A plot has to display in a
notebook. And gog's `+` has to work beside the operators the language
already has. Those are real questions, and answering them in the grammar
chapters would answer them wrongly for three readers out of four.

All four bindings work, so all four have a chapter here
[@rcore2026; @vanrossum2009python; @bezanson2017julia; @ecma2025javascript].
None of them required the grammar chapters to be rewritten: that is the reason
for keeping this part separate.

They are ordered R, Python, Julia, JavaScript, and the order has a reason. The
first three write the same sentence three times: the operators are identical, and
the only thing that moves is how a column is named, from a bare `gdp` to `col.gdp`
to `:gdp`. If you have read the R in this book you can read the Python and the
Julia already. JavaScript is the one that genuinely reads differently, because it
is the only one of the four that cannot give `+`, `*`, `|` and `/` new meanings, so
it spells them as words. It is last for that reason, not because it is the newest of the four.

The four chapters are also the proof. Every sentence in this book was
translated and drawn by every binding. The four produce byte-identical
plots and refuse the same sentences in the same words. They differ only
where a chapter is about the host language itself.
